Here's a comprehensive overview of **OpenCode** — the open-source AI coding agent — based on the search results:

---

## What is OpenCode?

OpenCode is a **free, open-source, terminal-based AI coding agent** (can be installed via `npm install -g opencode-ai`). It's model-agnostic, supporting **75+ LLM providers** (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, local models via Ollama, etc.), and runs on a "bring your own key" (BYOK) model — the software is free, you pay only for API token usage.

---

## ✅ Pros (Strengths)

| Pro | Details |
|---|---|
| **No vendor lock-in** | Switch between Claude, GPT, Gemini, or local models without changing your workflow. |
| **Multi-provider flexibility** | Route different tasks to different models (e.g., Claude Sonnet for complex refactoring, GPT-4o-mini for quick edits, Gemini Flash for search, local models for sensitive code). |
| **Open source transparency** | Every line of code is auditable — important for security-conscious teams. |
| **Privacy by default** | Use local models (Ollama, LM Studio) for code that cannot leave your machine. |
| **True agentic behavior** | It actually completes multi-step tasks, not just suggests code snippets. |
| **Cost predictable** | Pay per token, not a flat subscription. Light users can spend $5–20/month; using cheap models (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini Flash) keeps costs near zero. |
| **Polished TUI** | A keyboard-driven terminal UI with built-in editor, file change tracking, and session management. Also available as a desktop app and IDE extension. |
| **Dual-agent architecture** | Plan agent (read-only analysis, architectural strategy) + Build agent (executes changes). |
| **Auto Compact** | Intelligently summarizes conversation history to keep context windows small and costs predictable in long sessions. |
| **Active development** | Maintained by the SST team; moves fast with frequent updates. |

---

## ❌ Cons (Weaknesses)

| Con | Details |
|---|---|
| **Limited IDE integration** | Primarily a terminal tool — no inline code completion, graphical diff view, or polished IDE experience like Cursor. |
| **API costs can add up** | Heavy usage with Claude Opus or GPT-4 can exceed $20–50/month. |
| **Manual configuration required** | Does not work out of the box — you need to install, get API keys, create a config file, and set up provider routing. |
| **Learning curve** | Less hand-holding than commercial tools like Cursor or Claude Code. |
| **Smaller community** | Fewer tutorials, guides, and community-maintained configurations compared to Claude Code or Cursor. |
| **No built-in multi-agent orchestration** | Single-agent tool — cannot coordinate multiple agents working in parallel. |
| **Occasional hallucinations** | Like all LLM tools, it can confidently make wrong edits — always review changes. |
| **Documentation gaps** | Being open-source doesn't always mean well-documented. |

---

## 🆕 Recent Updates (v1.3.0+)

Based on the latest info (v1.3.3 as of 2026):

1. **Node.js support** (v1.3.0) — Previously required Bun; now runs on Node.js, resolving adoption blockers for corporate environments with strict runtime policies.

2. **xAI Responses API integration** — Improved reasoning performance for long multi-turn conversations, especially for Grok model users.

3. **Multistep Authentication** — Native support for complex enterprise SSO flows (e.g., GitHub Copilot for Enterprise), eliminating awkward API-key workarounds.

4. **Git-backed Session Review** — Visual diff and status map directly in the TUI, showing which files are being analyzed/edited and why.

5. **Auto Compact feature** — Intelligent summarization of long session histories to maintain low latency and predictable costs.

6. **Dual-agent architecture** (Plan + Build agents) — Separates intention from execution; Plan agent does read-only analysis before any writes happen.

---

## Pricing Overview

| Provider | Model | Input (1M tokens) | Output (1M tokens) | Typical Session Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anthropic | Claude Sonnet 4 | $3.00 | $15.00 | $0.10–0.50 |
| Anthropic | Claude Haiku 3.5 | $0.80 | $4.00 | $0.03–0.15 |
| OpenAI | GPT-4o | $2.50 | $10.00 | $0.08–0.40 |
| OpenAI | GPT-4o-mini | $0.15 | $0.60 | $0.01–0.05 |
| Google | Gemini 2.5 Flash | $0.15 | $0.60 | $0.01–0.05 |
| Local | CodeLlama (Ollama) | Free | Free | $0.00 |

---

## Bottom Line

**Best for:** Developers comfortable with the terminal who want flexibility, privacy, and cost control. Great for teams that need to audit their tools or use multiple AI providers.

**Not ideal for:** Beginners who prefer a polished GUI, or users who want a zero-setup "download and go" experience like Cursor.

Here are the results of the web search for **OpenCode (opencode-ai) v1.17.19** user feedback, reviews, and issues:

---

## 🚨 Key Issue: v1.17.19 Forced a New Layout That Broke Major Features

### Release Notes (v1.17.19)
The update introduced a **redesigned interface** (attachment cards, review panel, file browsing, Edit Project modal) and **auto-enabled a new "tabs on top" layout** — especially impactful for Web users.

### 🔴 Critical GitHub Issue [#37546](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/37546) — "No way to revert new layout on Web"

| Problem | Details |
|---|---|
| **No revert option on Web** | The "New layout" toggle in Settings → General is only shown when `layoutTransitionEligible` is set — and that flag is only populated by **desktop onboarding**, never on Web. |
| **Workspaces/worktrees completely missing** | The new layout (`layout-new.tsx`) is a bare shell with no projects sidebar. The workspaces feature only exists in the legacy layout. Upgrading silently **loses the feature** with no recovery path. |
| **Mobile users locked in** | Running `opencode serve` and accessing via phone? You can't open DevTools on mobile Safari/Chrome, so the `localStorage` workaround is unreachable. No tap target, no command palette entry, no settings row. |
| **Agent selector button gone** | Since v1.15.6 (#28769), the agent selector button disappeared from the composer. Switching agents now requires typing `/agent name` each session. |
| **"Plan/Build" pill vanished** | The agent pill disappeared in v1.15.9 (#28908) as part of desktop parity changes. |
| **Sunset date** | The old layout toggle is scheduled to be removed entirely by **2026-09-14**, but Web users currently have zero access to it. |

> *"A Web user who had workspaces enabled silently loses the feature with no in-app way to recover it."*

---

### 🗣️ Hacker News Discussion (strong community frustration)

A popular HN thread titled *"Annoying and alarming things about OpenCode"* (254 points, 174 comments) included:

- **"I updated one of my containers today and had to downgrade it back"** — Worktree/workspace support is gone, multiple sessions now require tabs, command palette is hotkey-only.
- **"Issues about the new design just sit in an endless unsolved pile on GitHub"** — Aggressive stale bot not helping.
- **"Codebase is hopelessly bloated by vibe coded features"** — Stability, performance, and memory use have all gotten worse.
- **"Pi has fully replaced it for me"** — Several users migrating to alternatives like `oh-my-pi` and other minimalist options.
- **Prompt cache misses** — The tool re-reads `AGENTS.md` on every SSE turn, and puts the current date in the system prompt causing full cache misses at midnight.
- **Compaction issues** — Users report compaction and pruning interact poorly and don't work well.

A developer from OpenCode responded: compaction is a "necessary evil" for context window limits, but **V2 (in beta)** has a new system for handling changing system instructions that avoids cache misses.

---

### Summary
**v1.17.19** is widely seen as a **regressive update** that forced a half-baked new UI layout on Web users, removed workspaces entirely, hid the revert toggle, and left mobile users with no escape hatch. The broader community sentiment ranges from frustration to migration away from the project due to bloat, instability, and slow resolution of critical issues.

- The `.analytics-grid` container (line 838) lays out its children with a two‑column CSS grid:

```css
.analytics-grid {

```

- Each `.analytics-card` simply fills the grid cell (no explicit width).

```css
@media (max-width: 1400px) {
  .analytics-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
}
```

That means on most desktop‑size viewports the cards already sit side‑by‑side, but once the viewport narrows they stack vertically. The “compact” feel can be influenced by three main parameters:

1. **Column count / width** – Keep two columns but shrink each column a bit for a denser layout.  
2. **Gap size** – Reduce `gap` (currently `var(--space-4)` → 16 px) to bring the cards closer together.  
3. **Card padding / element sizing** – Lower the internal padding, font sizes, and chart height so each card occupies less vertical space.

**Straight‑forward suggestions (no code changes needed right now)**

| Goal | How to achieve it (conceptually) |
|------|----------------------------------|
| **Keep cards side‑by‑side on more screen sizes** | Raise the breakpoint that forces a single column (e.g., change `max-width: 1400px` to `max-width: 1200px` or lower). This keeps the two‑column grid on slightly narrower windows. |
| **Make the layout feel more compact** | Decrease the grid gap from `var(--space-4)` (16 px) to `var(--space-3)` (12 px) or even `var(--space-2)` (8 px). That pulls the cards closer together without altering the design tokens elsewhere. |
| **Compress each card’s visual weight** | Reduce the internal padding on `.analytics-card-header` and `.analytics-card-body` (they’re currently `var(--space-4)` / `var(--space-5)`). A smaller padding (e.g., `var(--space-3)`) shortens the card’s height. |
| **Shrink chart height** | The chart wrapper (`.analytics-chart-wrapper`) is set to `height: 220px`. Lowering that to, say, `180px` makes the card’s body slimmer while preserving readability. |
| **Adjust font sizing for compact mode** | If you want a globally “compact” feel, you can toggle the `[data-compact="true"]` mode (the stylesheet already defines tighter token values). Adding `data-compact="true"` to the `<html>` element makes all font‑sizes, spacing, and component dimensions shrink uniformly, which includes the analytics cards. |
| **Optional flex‑based layout** | If you’d rather use Flexbox (e.g., for equal‑height cards that wrap cleanly), you could replace the `display: grid` on `.analytics-grid` with `display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: var(--space-3);`. Each card would then need a `flex: 1 1 calc(50% - var(--gap))` rule, but this is a larger structural change. |

**What to try first**

1. **Reduce the gap** – Change the `gap` on `.analytics-grid` from `var(--space-4)` to `var(--space-3)`. That’s the smallest tweak and instantly brings the cards visually closer together.
2. **Adjust the breakpoint** – If you see the cards stacking too early, modify the media query that collapses the grid (`@media (max-width: 1400px)`). A tighter limit like `1100px` will preserve the side‑by‑side layout on more mid‑size screens.
3. **Enable compact mode** – Adding `data-compact="true"` to the `<html>` tag will apply a whole set of token overrides that already exist in the stylesheet (spacing, font sizes, radii). This is a one‑line change that makes the entire UI denser, including the analytics cards.
